intro.title: Matrices
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **matrix** is a grid of values that are all the same type, with rows and columns. It is like a data frame where every column is numbers, and it is how R stores things like counts by two categories. `matrix()` fills it **column by column** from a vector:

```
sales <- matrix(
  c(12, 8, 5, 15, 6, 7, 10, 9, 4, 18, 7, 8, 20, 11, 9),
  nrow = 3,
  dimnames = list(c("latte", "tea", "mocha"), c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"))
)
sales
```

`dimnames` gives the rows and columns names (a list: row names first, then column names). Add `byrow = TRUE` to fill row by row instead. `dim(sales)` gives the size: 3 rows, 5 columns.

Pick values with `[row, column]`, by position or by name, just like a data frame: `sales["tea", "Wed"]`, `sales[1, ]` (a whole row), `sales[, "Fri"]` (a whole column).

| Function | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `rowSums(m)`, `rowMeans(m)` | one value per row |
| `colSums(m)`, `colMeans(m)` | one value per column |
| `t(m)` | the matrix turned on its side: rows become columns |
| `rbind(m, new)`, `cbind(m, new)` | a new row or column added |

Maths on a matrix works value by value, like a vector: `sales * 2` doubles every count. A vector as long as the number of rows is reused down each column, so it lines up with the rows: `sales * c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2)` multiplies each drink's counts by its price.

intro.title: apply() over rows and columns
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`rowSums()` and `colMeans()` cover sums and means. For anything else, such as the best score per test or each student's range, `apply()` runs a function on every row or every column of a matrix:

```
scores <- matrix(
  c(72, 65, 88, 54, 78, 70, 85, 61, 81, 68, 90, 59),
  nrow = 4,
  dimnames = list(c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee"), c("t1", "t2", "t3"))
)
apply(scores, 2, max)    # 2: each column, so each test
apply(scores, 1, max)    # 1: each row, so each student
```

The middle argument is the **margin**: `1` for rows, `2` for columns, the same as in `prop.table()`. The function can be your own, written in place: `apply(scores, 1, function(x) max(x) - min(x))` is each student's range.

If the function gives one value, `apply()` gives a vector, named by the rows or columns. If it gives several, such as `range()`, the result is a matrix with one **column** per row or column you applied it to, which often needs a `t()` to read.

Extra arguments go after the function, as with `sapply()`: `apply(m, 2, mean, na.rm = TRUE)`.

`apply()` also works on a data frame of numbers (it turns it into a matrix first), but a data frame with text columns becomes a text matrix, so pick the number columns first.

intro.title: Split, apply, combine
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Many questions follow the same three steps: **split** the data into groups, **apply** something to each group, and **combine** the answers. `tapply()` does all three for one column and one summary. When you need more, do the steps yourself.

`split(x, g)` splits a vector into a **list**, one item per group. `split(df, df$g)` splits a whole data frame into a list of smaller data frames:

```
deliveries <- data.frame(
  rider = c("Sam", "Ola", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Kit", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit"),
  area = c("north", "south", "north", "north", "south", "south", "north", "south", "south", "north", "north", "south"),
  minutes = c(24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 29, 22, 74, 33, 21, 26, 38)
)
by_rider <- split(deliveries$minutes, deliveries$rider)
by_rider$Ola                   # 31 27 74 26
parts <- split(deliveries, deliveries$area)
parts$north                    # the north rows, all columns
```

Then apply with `sapply()` (one value per group) or `lapply()` (anything per group). Inside, each group is a normal vector or data frame:

```
sapply(by_rider, mean)
sapply(parts, function(d) d$rider[which.max(d$minutes)])    # slowest rider in each area
```

To **combine** a list of data frames into one, stack them with `do.call(rbind, list_of_frames)`. `do.call()` calls a function with the items of a list as its arguments, so it is the same as `rbind(list[[1]], list[[2]], …)` however many there are.

```
rows <- lapply(names(parts), function(a) data.frame(area = a, n = nrow(parts[[a]]), mean = mean(parts[[a]]$minutes)))
do.call(rbind, rows)
```

intro.title: Sets and match()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Before combining tables, and after, you often ask questions about **sets** of values: who is in both clubs, which codes are new, which orders aren't on the menu. R has a function for each:

```
chess <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy")
choir <- c("Cy", "Dee", "Ana", "Eli")
union(chess, choir)        # in either: Ana Ben Cy Dee Eli
intersect(chess, choir)    # in both: Ana Cy
setdiff(chess, choir)      # in chess but not choir: Ben
```

Each gives every value once, in the order it first appears. `setdiff()` is one-sided: `setdiff(choir, chess)` is Dee and Eli.

`match(x, table)` gives, for each value of `x`, its **position** in `table`, or NA if it isn't there. That makes it a quick lookup: use the positions to pick from another column of the same table.

```
menu <- data.frame(drink = c("latte", "tea", "mocha", "chai"), price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2, 3.8))
orders <- c("tea", "latte", "latte", "flat white", "chai")
match(orders, menu$drink)                  # 2 1 1 NA 4
menu$price[match(orders, menu$drink)]      # the price of each order
```

This is what `merge()` does under the hood, but `match()` keeps the orders in their own order, one result per order, with NA for anything unknown, which makes the gaps easy to find.

intro.title: Stacking tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Data often arrives in pieces: one sheet per shop, per month or per class. To analyse it, stack the pieces into one table with `rbind()`. Three school shops sent in their sales:

```
shop_a <- data.frame(item = c("mug", "tote"), sold = c(5, 3))
shop_b <- data.frame(sold = c(4, 6), item = c("mug", "poster"))
shop_c <- data.frame(item = "mug", sold = 2, price = 8.5)
```

`rbind(shop_a, shop_b)` works even though `shop_b` has its columns the other way round: for data frames, `rbind()` matches columns **by name**. But `rbind(shop_a, shop_c)` stops with an error, because `shop_c` has an extra `price` column. Give the others that column first, as NA: `shop_a$price <- NA`.

Once stacked, you can no longer tell which row came from which shop, so add a column saying so **before** stacking: `shop_a$shop <- "A"`.

`cbind()` is the sideways version: it puts columns next to each other, matching rows by position, so the rows must already be in the same order.

For many pieces in a list, `do.call(rbind, pieces)` stacks them all. The row names it makes, like `sep.1`, can be cleared with `rownames(x) <- NULL`.

intro.title: Joining on keys
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The Data frames quest used `merge()` to join two tables on a shared column. Real joins raise more questions: what if the key columns have different names, what if a key appears more than once, and what about rows that don't match? A school keeps three tables:

```
pupils <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 3, 4), name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee"), class = c("7A", "7B", "7A", "7B"))
clubs <- data.frame(pupil = c(1, 1, 3, 5), club = c("chess", "choir", "choir", "drama"))
tutors <- data.frame(class = c("7A", "7B"), tutor = c("Ms Obi", "Mr Lund"))
```

When the key has a different name in each table, say which is which: `merge(pupils, clubs, by.x = "id", by.y = "pupil")`.

Ana is in two clubs, so she appears **twice** in the result: each pupil row is matched with every club row that has the same key. That is usually what you want (one row per pupil and club), but a key repeated by mistake, such as a tutor listed twice, quietly multiplies rows. Check keys with `duplicated()` before joining.

| Argument | Keeps |
| --- | --- |
| (none) | only rows that match in both |
| `all.x = TRUE` | every row of the first table, with NA where nothing matched |
| `all.y = TRUE` | every row of the second table |
| `all = TRUE` | every row of both |

To find what doesn't match, use `%in%`: `clubs[!clubs$pupil %in% pupils$id, ]` is a club row for a pupil who isn't on the list. When a match needs two columns, such as class **and** term, give both: `by = c("class", "term")`.

intro.title: Wide and long
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The same data can be laid out two ways. This rainfall table is **wide**: one row per town, one column per month. It is easy to read, but awkward to analyse: "total per month" means working across columns, and adding April means adding a column.

```
rain <- data.frame(
  town = c("Ashby", "Brook", "Corran"),
  jan = c(80, 65, 92),
  feb = c(60, 55, 71),
  mar = c(55, 48, 60)
)
```

The **long** layout has one row per measurement: a town column, a month column and one column of values. Grouping, filtering and stacking new data all become the tools you already know:

```
long <- data.frame(
  town = rep(rain$town, times = 3),
  month = rep(c("jan", "feb", "mar"), each = 3),
  mm = c(rain$jan, rain$feb, rain$mar)
)
tapply(long$mm, long$month, sum)
```

Building it by hand, as above, shows exactly what happens: `rep(…, times = 3)` repeats the towns for each month and `rep(…, each = 3)` repeats each month for the three towns. Base R also has `reshape()`, which does it in one call (its arguments take some getting used to), and `stack()` for the quick case:

```
reshape(rain, direction = "long", varying = c("jan", "feb", "mar"), v.names = "mm",
        timevar = "month", times = c("jan", "feb", "mar"), idvar = "town")
stack(rain[, c("jan", "feb", "mar")])    # columns values and ind
```

To go back to wide, `reshape(long, direction = "wide", idvar = "town", timevar = "month")` gives columns `mm.jan`, `mm.feb`, `mm.mar`. For a grid of numbers, `tapply(long$mm, list(long$town, long$month), sum)` gives a matrix. Text columns become alphabetical, so make month a factor with `levels = c("jan", "feb", "mar")` to keep calendar order.

intro.title: Tables into data frames
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`table()`, `tapply()` and `sapply()` give named vectors and tables: good to look at, awkward to sort, join or add columns to. Turning them into data frames lets you carry on with everything from the Data frames quest.

`as.data.frame()` turns a table of counts into a data frame with one row per value and a `Freq` column. Name the variable inside `table()` and the column gets that name:

```
orders <- data.frame(
  order = 101:110,
  day = c("Mon", "Mon", "Tue", "Tue", "Tue", "Wed", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Fri"),
  drink = c("latte", "tea", "mocha", "latte", "latte", "tea", "chai", "latte", "mocha", "tea"),
  size = c("M", "S", "L", "M", "S", "M", "L", "L", "M", "S"),
  price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2, 3.4, 2.9, 2.5, 3.8, 3.9, 4.2, 2.2)
)
as.data.frame(table(drink = orders$drink))
```

A two-way table becomes one row per **combination**, including the ones with a count of 0, which is the long layout from the Wide and long stage. `xtabs(Freq ~ day + size, data = df)` turns it back into a table.

A named vector, such as the result of `tapply()`, becomes a data frame with the names as one column and the values as another:

```
totals <- tapply(orders$price, orders$drink, sum)
data.frame(drink = names(totals), total = as.vector(totals))
```

Once both are data frames, `merge()` puts them together: counts and takings per drink in one table, ready to sort and report.

challenges.title: Expert: The region report
challenges.promptMarkdown:
Show one line per region with the number of readings (not counting NAs) and the mean, rounded to 1 decimal place:

```
north: 5 readings, mean 10.9
south: 5 readings, mean 14.1
```

challenges.solution:
temps <- data.frame(
  station = c("N1", "N2", "S1", "S2"),
  d1 = c(11.2, 10.8, 14.1, 13.6),
  d2 = c(12.0, NA, 14.8, 14.2),
  d3 = c(10.5, 10.1, 13.9, NA)
)
stations <- data.frame(
  station = c("N1", "N2", "S1", "S2", "S3"),
  region = c("north", "north", "south", "south", "south"),
  altitude = c(120, 340, 15, 60, 30)
)
long <- data.frame(
  station = rep(temps$station, times = 3),
  day = rep(c("d1", "d2", "d3"), each = 4),
  temp = c(temps$d1, temps$d2, temps$d3)
)
joined <- merge(long, stations, by = "station")
parts <- split(joined$temp, joined$region)
for (reg in names(parts)) {
  t <- parts[[reg]][!is.na(parts[[reg]])]
  cat(reg, ": ", length(t), " readings, mean ", round(mean(t), 1), "\n", sep = "")
}

questions.prompt: Why turn the wide sheet long before joining the station details?

choices.label: Then each reading is a row, and region, day and station are all ordinary columns to group by

questions.explanation: Wide data could be joined too, but every summary would then work across columns.

questions.prompt: What does a plain `merge()` do with station S3, which has no readings?
questions.explanation: That is why `setdiff()` is worth running: missing stations don't show up by themselves.

questions.prompt: What does `mean(c(10.8, NA, 10.1), na.rm = TRUE)` give?
questions.explanation: The NA is left out, so it is the mean of two values.

questions.prompt: The correlation of station mean and altitude is −0.87. What does it suggest?

choices.label: Higher stations tend to be cooler, though 4 stations is very few

questions.explanation: And the north stations are higher, so region and altitude are mixed together.

questions.prompt: Why use `match()` to line up the altitudes with `station_means`?

choices.label: So each mean gets its own station's altitude, whatever the order of the two tables

questions.explanation: Lining up by position alone would be a silent mistake if the orders differed.

questions.prompt: Which function finds the stations in the details table that sent no readings?
questions.explanation: `setdiff(stations$station, temps$station)`
